title: Citi restricts AI agents from accessing customer accounts
content:
Photo: Steve A Johnson / Pexels
Citi restricts AI agents from accessing customer accounts
The bank is drawing hard lines around autonomous AI as Wall Street grows wary of software that can move money on its own
Citi is restricting AI agents from accessing customer accounts, according to the Financial Times.
The clearest window into Citi’s thinking came from CEO Jane Fraser at Sibos 2026 in Miami on September 30, 2026. Sibos is the annual banking and payments conference.
Fraser argued that autonomous AI agents need rigorous identity verification and authentication before they can execute transactions. That applies whether the agent is acting for a customer or for the bank itself.
Fraser said she was confident Citi could avoid the risks that come with uncontrolled agents. Her centerpiece was ARC, an internal platform Citi uses to monitor and govern AI agents.
“You cannot create an agent without going through ARC.”
ARC was introduced in 2026 and is mandatory for overseeing all of Citi’s internal AI agents.
Citi has been gradually rolling out governed AI systems internally since at least mid-2025, with an emphasis on compliance and oversight.

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon went further during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call on October 13–15, 2026. Dimon declared a total ban on external AI agents accessing JPMorgan customer accounts. His stated concern was the danger of “rogue agents.”
There is a difference in emphasis between the two banks. Dimon publicly prohibited third-party agents outright. Fraser’s public remarks have centered on strict internal governance rather than announcing an equivalent blanket ban on outside agents.
For companies building agentic AI tools for personal finance, this is a meaningful headwind. Many of the most compelling use cases involve an agent that can see and act on a user’s bank accounts. If the largest banks wall off customer accounts, those products lose access to a big chunk of the market.
For the banks themselves, governance isn’t free. Platforms like ARC require staff, systems, and ongoing monitoring.
Fraser’s emphasis on identity verification hints that the issue isn’t agents per se, but unverified ones. Unlike JPMorgan, Citi has avoided a public ban on external agents, instead focusing on internal controls.

report.summary: Citi is restricting AI agents from customer accounts, requiring rigorous identity verification and internal governance through its ARC platform, as Wall Street grows wary of autonomous money-moving software.
report.background: Banks have experimented with AI for compliance and customer service since at least 2025, but agentic AI that can independently initiate transactions raises new risks around fraud, liability, and control. Citi's ARC platform, mandatory for all internal AI agents since 2026, reflects a governance-first approach. CEO Jane Fraser used Sibos 2026 to argue that agents need verifiable identity before executing transactions, whether acting for customers or the bank. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon went further, banning external AI agents from customer accounts during the bank's Q3 2026 earnings call, citing 'rogue agents.' The split highlights an industry-wide debate: block third-party agents outright or govern them with strict authentication. For fintech startups building agentic personal finance tools, bank account access is often essential, making these policies a major market barrier.
key_points: Citi is not banning all AI agents outright; it is restricting them from customer accounts unless they pass rigorous identity verification and authentication, with CEO Jane Fraser saying agents must be verified before executing transactions.

The bank's internal ARC platform is mandatory: 'You cannot create an agent without going through ARC.' ARC monitors and governs all of Citi's internal AI agents, introduced in 2026 to enforce compliance and oversight.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon went further, declaring a total ban on external AI agents accessing JPMorgan customer accounts, citing 'rogue agents.' Citi has avoided an equivalent public ban on third-party agents.

For fintechs building agentic AI for personal finance, the moves are a significant headwind. Many compelling use cases require an agent to see and act on a user's bank accounts, so walled-off accounts shrink the addressable market.
Governance is costly: platforms like ARC demand dedicated staff, systems, and continuous monitoring. Banks must balance innovation in agentic AI against reputational, regulatory, and financial risk.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Citi and JPMorgan signal that autonomous agents touching money will face identity, authentication, and audit requirements before scale. Developers building agentic finance tools must design for bank-grade verification, least-privilege access, and human-in-the-loop controls, or risk losing access to major institutions. Regular users may see fewer seamless AI money-management products, but stronger protections against rogue or compromised agents. Banks gain control but bear higher governance costs. The broader lesson: agentic AI adoption in regulated finance will likely be gated by identity and policy infrastructure, not raw model capability. Startups that solve verifiable agent identity and permissioning may find opportunity.
report.tools: Watch agent governance and identity projects: SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity, Open Policy Agent (OPA) for policy enforcement, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect for delegated authorization, and LangChain, CrewAI, or Microsoft AutoGen for building agents with guardrails. Also follow Citi's ARC as a proprietary benchmark, and emerging agent identity standards from the Cloud Security Alliance and FIDO Alliance.
